L25@P0: a b s t r a c t
L26@P0: Discrimination of plant species in the optical reflective domain is somewhat limited by the similarity
L27@P0: of their reflectance spectra. Spectral characteristics in the visible to shortwave infrared (VSWIR) consist of combination bands and overtones of primary absorption bands, situated in the Thermal Infrared
L28@P0: (TIR) region and therefore resulting in broad spectral features. TIR spectroscopy is assumed to have
L29@P0: a large potential for providing complementary information to VSWIR spectroscopy. So far, in the TIR,
L30@P0: plants were often considered featureless. Recently and following advances in sensor technology, plant
L31@P0: species were discriminated based on specific emissivity signatures by Ullah et al.(2012) using directionalhemispherical reflectance (DHR) measurements in the laboratory. Here we examine if an accurate
L32@P0: discrimination of plant species is equally possible using emissive thermal infrared imaging spectroscopy,
L33@P0: an explicit spatial technique that is faster and more flexible than non-imaging measurements.
L34@P0: Hyperspectral thermal infrared images were acquired in the 7.8–11.56 m range at 40 nm spectral
L35@P0: resolution (@10 m) using a TIR imaging spectrometer (Telops HyperCam-LW) on seven plants each, of
L36@P0: eight different species. The images were radiometrically calibrated and subjected to temperature and
L37@P0: emissivity separation using a spectral smoothness approach. First, retrieved emissivity spectra were
L38@P0: compared to laboratory reference spectra and then subjected to species discrimination using a random
L39@P0: forest classifier. Second, classification results obtained with emissivity spectra were compared to those
L40@P0: obtained with VSWIR reflectance spectra that had been acquired from the same leaf samples.
L41@P0: In general, the mean emissivity spectra measured by the TIR imaging spectrometer showed very good
L42@P0: agreement with the reference spectra (average Nash-Sutcliffe-Efficiency Index = 0.64). In species discrimination, the resulting accuracies for emissivity spectra are highly dependent on the signal-to-noise
L43@P0: ratio (SNR). At high SNR, the TIR data (Overall Accuracy (OAA) = 92.26%) outperformed the VSWIR data
L44@P0: (OAA= 80.28%).
L45@P0: This study demonstrates that TIR imaging spectroscopy allows for fast and spatial measurements of
L46@P0: spectral plant emissivity with accuracies comparable to laboratory measurement. This innovative technique offers a valuable addition to VSWIR spectroscopy as it provides complimentary information for
L47@P0: plant species discrimination.

L49@P0: 1. Introduction
L50@P0: Vegetation mapping and species discrimination are key
L51@P0: requirements of studies focusing on ecosystem monitoring and

L54@P0: development. The time consuming traditional methods of infield mapping are optimized by remote sensing data collection,
L55@P0: which facilitates the economic acquisition of repeated data products allowing for large area studies of vegetation cover (Langley
L56@P0: et al., 2001). Remote sensing based vegetation mapping has been

L73@P1: The measurements for the species discrimination experiment took place on August 21st and 22nd 2013 from 10:30 to 18:00 local time.
L74@P1: Multispectral and hyperspectral systems in the visible to shortwave infrared (VSWIR; 0.4–2.5 m) spectral range demonstrated
L75@P1: their capability in plant discrimination (Govender et al., 2007; Ustin
L76@P1: and Gamon, 2010). This is caused by the fact that the spectral features in the VSWIR are mostly defined by plant constituents such
L77@P1: as pigments, leaf water content and other biochemicals like lignin,
L78@P1: cellulose (Asner, 1998). Vegetation classification is facilitated by
L79@P1: the extraction of distinct and characteristic spectral features in the
L80@P1: VSWIR, such as green peak, red edge, and water absorption bands
L81@P1: (Asner, 1998; Govender et al., 2007).
L82@P1: While VSWIR spectra have been widely used for many different applications at laboratory to spaceborne levels, the use of the
L83@P1: thermal infrared spectral domain (TIR; 8–14 m) is not as widely
L84@P1: spread. The reasons for this are the lack of available spectrometers and the general low SNR in combination with subtle spectral
L85@P1: features, which had limited the benefits of TIR spectrometers in
L86@P1: the past (Ribeiro da Luz and Crowley, 2007). However, sensor
L87@P1: technology has improved in the past years and high resolution
L88@P1: spectrometersbecame available for laboratory,in-situandevenairborne applications. The increasing availability for commercial TIR
L89@P1: imaging spectrometers (e.g., Telops HyperCam-LW, Itres TASI-600,
L90@P1: Specim AisaOWL) in the last years underline the growing scientific
L91@P1: community and the rising number of studies using thermal infrared
L92@P1: imaging spectroscopy (Danilina et al., 2012; Vaughan et al., 2003).
L93@P1: Spectral characteristics in the VSWIR consist of combination
L94@P1: bands andovertones ofprimary absorptionbands resulting inbroad
L95@P1: spectral features. As many of the fundamental absorption bands
L96@P1: are situated in the TIR region, thermal infrared spectroscopy is
L97@P1: assumed to have a large potential for providing complementary
L98@P1: information to VSWIR spectroscopy, e.g. identification of vegetation and the quantification of leaf constituents (Ribeiro da Luz,
L99@P1: 2006; Silverstein et al., 2005). Despite the general meaning, a few
L100@P1: authors demonstrated that vegetation spectra in the TIR are different from blackbody (BB) signatures (Salisbury, 1986; Salisbury
L101@P1: and D’Aria, 1992). Moreover, just very recently it could be impressively demonstrated that plant species are discriminable in the TIR
L102@P1: (Ribeiro da Luz, 2006; Ullah et al., 2012b). Ullah et al. (2012b) and
L103@P1: Fabre et al. (2011) showed that the mid-wave infrared (MWIR;
L104@P1: 3–5 m) is sensitive towards leaf water content and Buitrago et al.
L105@P1: (2016) even demonstrated that multiple types of stress could be
L106@P1: spectrally identified. These studies were laboratory-based directional hemispherical reflectance (DHR) measurements of single
L107@P1: leaves. The results from active DHR spectroscopy can be adapted to
L108@P1: passive acquisition techniques used for remote sensing purposes
L109@P1: considering Kirchhoff’s law. However, these laboratory measurements are time consuming (40 min or longer for each analysis) and
L110@P1: only allow for a single, non-imaging leaf measurement at a time
L111@P1: (Hecker et al., 2011).
L112@P1: Ribeiro da Luz and Crowley (2007) collected in-situ vegetation
L113@P1: emissivity spectra using a passive non-imaging field spectrometer
L114@P1: and recognized spectral features identified in laboratory measurements carried out before. Beyond this, new developments in
L115@P1: emissive TIR spectroscopy focusing on hyperspectral TIR cameras
L116@P1: offer the possibilities for fast and spatial measurements of plant
L117@P1: emissivity. Nevertheless, the accuracy of such measurements and
L118@P1: their suitability for species discrimination at field conditions has
L119@P1: not been tested yet.
L120@P1: 2. Objectives
L121@P1: The overall aim of this study was to investigate if plant species
L122@P1: discrimination is feasible using emissive TIR imaging spectroscopy.
L123@P1: Specific objectives were to: i) compare emissivity spectra from
L124@P1: a passive emissive imaging spectrometer with reference spectra
L125@P1: from laboratory DHR measurements, ii) classify plant species using
L126@P1: the emissivity spectra as input, iii) compare classification accuracies of emissivity spectra with reflectance spectra from a traditional
L127@P1: VSWIR spectrometer, iv) demonstrate the ability of identifying
L128@P1: spatial heterogeneities using a TIR imaging spectrometer and v)
L129@P1: perform a systematic investigation on the effect of SNR on classification results.
L130@P1: 3. Methods
L131@P1: During summer 2013, an experiment was carried out in the
L132@P1: greenhouse facilities at Trier University. The greenhouse setup
L133@P1: allowed plants to be grown under controlled conditions and thermal hyperspectral measurements to be performed next to the
L134@P1: greenhouse under clear sky conditions.
L135@P1: 3.1. Species discrimination experiment
L136@P1: Eight different plant species were selected for this study
L137@P1: (Table 1). Five of the eight species are identical to those used by
L138@P1: Ullah et al. (2012b) and represent a wide range of leaves’ properties (i.e., colour, thickness, structure, shape) and different canopy
L139@P1: structures withexpectedvariations inemissivity. This species setup
L140@P1: allows for direct comparison with the results of Ullah et al. (2012b)
L141@P1: who assessed plant species discrimination in the thermal spectral
L142@P1: region in a laboratory experiment using active DHR spectroscopy.
L143@P1: Seven individual plants from each species were obtained from a
L144@P1: local nursery (n = 56). Emissivity measurements of five leaves were
L145@P1: taken of each plant, resulting in a total amount of 280 emissivity
L146@P1: spectra.
L147@P1: 3.2. Thermal infrared
L148@P1: 3.2.1. Thermal infrared spectroscopy
L149@P1: Infrared spectroscopy is an analytical technique that is based on
L150@P1: vibrational motions within molecules of matters that interact with
L151@P1: electromagnetic radiation (Christensen et al., 2000; Hecker et al.,
L152@P1: 2011). A molecule starts vibrating at fundamental frequency when
L153@P1: it is stimulated by absorption of specific electromagnetic radiation.
L154@P1: The frequency of such molecular vibration is characteristic for a
L155@P1: specific functional group and depends on the atoms’ masses and
L156@P1-2: the molecule’s geometry. If a molecule absorbs higher amounts of18 G. Rock et al. / International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation 53 (2016) 16–26
L157@P2: energy,the molecule is excited in overtones or combinations offundamental vibration frequencies (Wilson et al., 1955). Whereas NIR
L158@P2: and SWIR radiation (0.8–2.5 m) can excite molecules to overtone
L159@P2: vibrations, the midwave and longwave infrared spectral region
L160@P2: (2.5–25 m) may be used to study the fundamental vibrations and
L161@P2: associated molecular structures and can be used as a diagnostic tool
L162@P2: (Christensen et al., 2000; Salisbury, 1986).
L163@P2: The fundamental vibration frequencies of many constituents
L164@P2: composing the superficial epidermal layer of plant leaves are
L165@P2: situated in the TIR spectral region. Among others, cellulose,
L166@P2: hemicellulose, varieties of pectin and aromatic compounds have
L167@P2: characteristic features in the 8–2 m spectral range (Elvidge, 1988;
L168@P2: Ribeiro da Luz and Crowley, 2007; Riederer and Muller, 2006; Ullah
L169@P2: et al., 2012a). This is why TIR spectroscopy is assumed to have large
L170@P2: potential for identification of species specific surface compositions
L171@P2: and species discrimination.

L173@P2: infrared spectroscopy data, this study focuses on a passive acquisition technique. Passive measurements of emitted thermal infrared
